findings.title: The web client reads server chunks with no admission gate
evidence: libVELA/vela-wasm-bridge/src/lib.rs has no admitted-chunk export (the only chunk entry points are encrypt_vault_chunk_json:343 and decrypt_vault_chunk_json:350)
webVELA/src/main.ts:478-484 decrypts each chunk with `authed.epoch`
webVELA/src/api.ts:148 sets `this.epoch = m.epoch` from the server's own sync-manifest response
webVELA/src/main.ts:477 `if (!ct) continue` silently drops a chunk the server did not return
findings.detail: plan_chunk_download, plan_sync_epoch_match and the sealed-header gate are never reached on the web path. Epoch agreement is with a server-supplied number, and there is no per-chunk baseline. This is the same rollback class the mobile bridges close (18-mobile-sync-admission.md). N5-N7 must treat the web client as a caller that does not reach admission at all.

findings.title: The sealed-ciphertext gate lives only in the Android/Apple bridges
evidence: libVELA/vela-android-bridge/src/lib.rs:1011 `if !aead::is_sealed(blob)`
libVELA/vela-apple-bridge/src/lib.rs:1160 same check, duplicated
libVELA/vela-crypto/src/aead.rs:55-66 open_vault_chunk decrypts an unsealed blob and ignores chunk_id/lamport
desktopVELA/vela-desktop-core/src/sync.rs:1090 calls open_fleet_chunk directly with no is_sealed check
findings.detail: Two consequences. (a) N2 cannot reduce either bridge to type conversion while the gate stays there: it has to move into vela-sync-policy or vela-crypto first. (b) The desktop path, which is the reference implementation for the other clients, accepts a pre-C-2 unsealed chunk relabelled to any clock: reject_rollback (sync.rs:526) passes whenever the attacker-supplied clock is >= the recorded floor, and the open then ignores the label. The mobile gate stops exactly this; desktop does not.

findings.title: aad_binding_verified is a caller-supplied constant on the desktop path
evidence: desktopVELA/vela-desktop-core/src/sync.rs:531-538 reject_rollback passes aad_binding_verified: true and key_epoch_positive: true as literals
desktopVELA/vela-desktop-core/src/sync.rs:1086 calls reject_rollback *before* the AEAD open at :1090
findings.detail: On mobile the flag is set after a successful open (android:1069, apple:1200). On desktop it is an assumption asserted before decryption, i.e. the fact 17-universal-chunk-admission.md explicitly says its theorem does not establish. Desktop also never calls plan_sync_epoch_match.

findings.title: Android passkey primitives are a hand-mirrored copy, not a delegation
evidence: libVELA/vela-android-bridge/src/passkey.rs:1-27 states the WebAuthn layouts are 'line-for-line ports' of desktopVELA/vela-desktop-core/src/passkey.rs
libVELA/vela-android-bridge/src/passkey.rs uses p256/ciborium/sha2 directly; it never calls vela-core or vela-crypto
findings.detail: These four exports (and the Kotlin ceremony) cannot be proved to be thin wrappers because the logic is implemented twice. The desktop side additionally has a PresenceToken linear type that the JNI boundary cannot carry, so 'one ceremony per approval' is enforced in Kotlin.

findings.title: The user-verification decision crosses the Android boundary as an opaque int
evidence: androidVELA/.../security/passkey/PasskeyAuthenticator.kt:171-174 computes `flags = FLAG_UP or (if (verified) FLAG_UV else 0)` and passes it
libVELA/vela-android-bridge/src/lib.rs:599 nativePasskeyAuthDataJson forwards `flags` into the authenticator data
findings.detail: The WebAuthn UV bit, which RPs rely on, is decided in Kotlin from a `verified` boolean and is not checkable by the bridge. Any proof of the passkey path has to include the Kotlin caller, or the flag has to be derived natively.

findings.title: Neither mobile client uses the share pin, so share-envelope v2 forgery protection is inert on mobile
evidence: androidVELA/.../core/FeatureRepositories.kt:345-347 calls identityAdmitShare with no pin and no persisted SharePin anywhere in androidVELA
iosVELA/Sources/SharingViewModel.swift:51-53 calls identityAdmitShare without a pin
libVELA/vela-android-bridge/src/lib.rs:690 and the Apple twin accept an optional pin and the verified policy consumes it
findings.detail: Every mobile share admission is therefore 'first contact': the sender key is accepted and re-pinned per item. A sender-key swap for an existing lineage would be accepted. The desktop path does consult vela-client-share-policy with a stored generation (desktopVELA/vela-desktop-core/src/sharing.rs:195, :261, :784).

findings.title: Two mobile clients duplicate the epoch and manifest-floor decisions in native code
evidence: androidVELA/.../sync/VaultSyncManager.kt:43-49 requireMatchingSyncEpoch, called at :581, :627, :658; rejectRollback :912-924; requireReadableBaseline :927-933
iosVELA/Shared/SyncEngine.swift:298-302 epoch equality + rejectRollback (:233-249)
findings.detail: These are deliberate defence-in-depth (18-mobile-sync-admission.md calls the iOS manifest floor a stricter, fail-closed difference), but they mean the admission decision is not reachable only through the bridge: three implementations of the same predicate must stay in sync. N5-N7 should either prove them equivalent to the policy or retire them.

findings.title: Caller-supplied security facts pass straight through the bridges
evidence: recipient_bound is taken from the request and fed to the verified recovery policy: android lib.rs:1548, apple lib.rs:1317,1572
plan_recovery_publication: 12 caller booleans/ints (android lib.rs:1609, apple lib.rs:1508; Kotlin VaultSyncManager.kt:426, Swift AccountViewModel.swift:996)
desktop sync.rs:359 computes server_epoch_is_next itself and passes it to plan_epoch_adoption (noted as remaining caller-supplied in 18-mobile-sync-admission.md:65)
findings.detail: The verified kernels are only as strong as the facts handed to them, and these facts are observations the app claims to have made. N2/N5 must either derive them in Rust or state them as assumptions.

findings.title: Error identity is recovered by matching a Rust message substring
evidence: androidVELA/.../core/NativeVelaCore.kt:716-728 mapAdmittedChunkFailure matches 'legacy unsealed chunk ciphertext cannot be admitted'
iosVELA/Shared/SyncEngine.swift:319 does the same string match
findings.detail: The bridge returns {"error": "..."} with no machine-readable code, so both clients branch on English text. Any rewording in libVELA silently changes a security-relevant client behaviour.

findings.title: Error handling is inconsistent across the three bridges and their wrappers
evidence: Android: every JNI call returns JSON; Kotlin throws IllegalStateException (NativeVelaCore.kt:630-633)

Apple: most wrappers return nil on refusal (VelaCoreFFI.swift:41-62), so a rejected share and a missing handle are indistinguishable; only the admission path preserves the reason (AdmissionError.refused, :412-459)
WASM: {"error":...} is a successful call; only the TS wrapper turns it into a throw (webVELA/src/vela.ts:21-25)
findings.detail: N2's 'thin wrapper' property has to be stated per-platform because the failure channel differs, and any exhaustive caller analysis must model three different refusal semantics (Android's version and verification-code exports return bare strings, not error JSON).

findings.title: Bridge ABI divergences that make the two mobile bridges non-identical
evidence: signature key name: Android 'signature' (lib.rs:1232) vs Apple 'signature_b64' (lib.rs:877)
RMS capsule: Android requires exactly 32 bytes (lib.rs:1465) while Apple accepts >=32 and truncates (lib.rs:1236-1241)
open_rekey_capsule: Android takes previous_rms as a JSON int array (lib.rs:536) while Apple takes previous_rms_b64 as a string (lib.rs:892)
Apple alone exposes trusted-contact envelopes and possession proofs (lib.rs:674-711); Android alone exposes passkey primitives (lib.rs:586-635)
findings.detail: N2a-c cannot share one statement across the two bridges until these are reconciled; the truncation difference is the only one with a direct security reading.

findings.title: Dead and unreachable ABI surface
evidence: android C ABI vela_encrypt_bytes (lib.rs:885) has no caller anywhere, and returns no error message on failure
android nativeOpenRekeyCapsuleJson (lib.rs:569) has no Kotlin external
android Kotlin wrappers identityOpenShare (:363) and identityForgetAll (:439) have no caller
Apple vela_ffi_open_rekey_capsule_json, seal/open/seal_response contact-share, possession_proof, generate_recovery_request have no Swift wrapper
androidVELA LocalVaultRepository.decryptSyncedVault (:109) is the only user of the non-admitting chunk decrypt and has no caller
findings.detail: Harmless today, but each is a path on which a future caller can reach decryption without admission. N5-N7 should treat them as open doors rather than remove them silently.

unverified: JNI symbol resolution and jni crate behaviour were not executed (no build was run); the JNI names are read from source and matched by eye to com.vela.android.core.NativeVelaCore.
Swift was not compiled on this host; call-site analysis is textual.
The generated webVELA/src/wasm/*.js bindings are build artefacts and are not in the tree, so the TS <-> wasm calling convention is read from the #[wasm_bindgen] signatures only.
Whether any out-of-tree consumer (e.g. a published XCFramework consumer) calls the Apple exports with no Swift wrapper is unknown.
Desktop Tauri command count (109) is from attribute scanning; the gpui front end's 245 vela_desktop_core references were not individually classified.
